intro: Angels appear on greeting cards, tree ornaments and paintings. Most of those pictures show sweet babies with tiny wings. The Bible describes something very different. Its messengers are often strong and bright, and people who meet them are told, "Do not be afraid."

In this unit you will read what the Bible says about angels, with Michael Heiser as your guide. Heiser was a scholar who read the Bible in Hebrew and Greek. You will learn the words for messengers, cherubim and seraphim. You will meet Michael, Gabriel and Raphael. Then you will follow a puzzling figure called the Angel of the LORD, who speaks as if he were God.

By the end, you will be able to explain what the word angel means. You will be able to retell the stories of Hagar, Moses, Gideon and Samson's parents. You will also be able to describe Heiser's reading of the Angel of the LORD and at least one other way readers understand him.
bigQuestion: What does the Bible say angels are and do, and who is the Angel of the LORD who speaks as God?

timeline.t: Isaiah has his vision of the seraphim, in the year King Uzziah dies (Isaiah 6)
The Torah is put into Greek; the Hebrew mal'ak becomes angelos
The Book of Tobit, with the angel Raphael, is written
Luke and Hebrews are written; Gabriel visits Mary, and angels are called spirits who serve
Justin Martyr links the Angel of the LORD with the Son of God
The Mishnah is written down, including the rule that an agent is like the sender
Augustine writes that God may have spoken through created angels
Raphael paints little winged children, part of a trend that made baby angels popular
The King James Version of the Bible is published in English
Heiser publishes The Unseen Realm, with his two Yahwehs reading
Heiser publishes Angels, explaining that angel names a job
Michael Heiser dies; his books and podcast are still widely read and heard

words.d: a Hebrew word that means messenger, used for human and heavenly messengers
a Greek word that means messenger; the English word angel comes from it
a Bible name for heavenly beings, picturing them as members of God's household
the great crowd or army of heavenly beings around God's throne
powerful winged guardians of holy places, like Eden and the ark of the covenant
six-winged beings above God's throne in Isaiah 6 who call out that God is holy
a chief messenger; Jude 9 uses this title for Michael
books, like Tobit, that Protestants keep outside their canon but Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include
a figure in the Hebrew Bible who is sent by God but often speaks as God
the personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often printed LORD in English Bibles
Heiser's reading: God unseen in heaven and God seen, often as the Angel of the LORD
someone sent to act or speak for another; the Mishnah says an agent is like the sender

test.q: What do the Hebrew word mal'ak and the Greek word angelos both mean?
test.why: Both words mean messenger. Heiser stressed that angel names a job, not a kind of being.

test.q: In Genesis 32, who does the Hebrew word mal'ak describe?
choices: Both heavenly messengers and Jacob's human messengers
test.why: Genesis 32:1 uses mal'ak for messengers of God, and 32:3 uses it for the men Jacob sends to Esau.

test.q: Which beings sit on the cover of the ark of the covenant?
test.why: Exodus 25:18–22 describes two gold cherubim on the ark's cover.

test.q: Which beings in Isaiah 6 have six wings?
test.why: Isaiah 6:2 says each seraph has six wings.

test.q: Which angel is called the great prince in Daniel 12:1?
test.why: Daniel 12:1 calls Michael the great prince who stands up for Daniel's people.

test.q: In which Bibles is the Book of Tobit part of the Old Testament?
test.why: Tobit is in Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments. Protestants place it in the Apocrypha.

test.q: Where did the picture of chubby baby angels mostly come from?
choices: European paintings made long after the Bible
test.why: Painters in Italy, about five hundred years ago, made winged children popular. Bible angels often look like grown men.

test.q: Which verse describes angels as spirits who serve, sent to help?
test.why: Hebrews 1:14 calls angels serving spirits sent to help people.

test.q: What did Elisha's servant see when his eyes were opened in 2 Kings 6?
test.why: 2 Kings 6:17 says he saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.

test.q: In Genesis 16, what does Hagar call the one who spoke to her?
test.why: Genesis 16:13 says she called the LORD who spoke to her the God who sees me.

test.q: In Judges 6, what happens right after the angel greets Gideon?
choices: The text says the LORD turned to him and spoke
test.why: Judges 6:14 says the LORD turned to Gideon, right after the angel of the LORD had spoken.

test.q: What did Heiser mean by the two Yahwehs?
choices: Two gods of two different nations
God unseen in heaven and God seen, often as the Angel of the LORD
Two names for the angel Gabriel
Two copies of the Hebrew Bible
test.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser described God unseen and God seen as two Yahwehs.

test.q: What does Exodus 23:21 say is in the angel God sends?
test.why: Exodus 23:21 says, My name is in him.

test.q: How do Jewish readers usually explain the angel of the LORD?
choices: As a messenger or agent who speaks for God
test.why: Jewish readers usually see him as a messenger. The Mishnah teaches that an agent is like the one who sends him.

test.q: How did Augustine's view differ from Justin Martyr's?
choices: Augustine thought God may have spoken through created angels
Augustine rejected the Book of Genesis
Augustine said the angel was Gideon
test.why: Justin linked the appearances to the Son of God. Augustine thought God may have spoken through created angels.

write.prompt: Who is the Angel of the LORD? Choose two or three passages from this unit, such as Genesis 16:7–13, Exodus 3:2–6, Judges 6:11–24 or Exodus 23:20–21. Explain what each passage says. Then explain how Heiser read the Angel and how Jewish readers or another Christian reader, like Augustine, understood him.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse for every passage you use.
Say who holds each view: Heiser argues, Jewish readers explain, Augustine thought.
Compare the readings fairly. You do not need to pick a winner.
Use unit words like mal'ak, angel of the LORD, agent and two Yahwehs.
